nameStory: Radiofilum gets its name from the Latin 'radius' meaning ray or spoke, and 'filum' meaning thread - describing how this tiny algae forms radiating thread-like filaments that spread outward like spokes on a wheel. The species name 'conjunctivum' means 'joined together,' referring to how the cells connect end-to-end in delicate chains.
description: Radiofilum conjunctivum is a microscopic freshwater green algae that forms delicate, thread-like filaments in quiet waters. These tiny organisms create wispy, hair-thin strands that can sometimes be seen with the naked eye as gossamer threads floating just below the water surface. Individual filaments are incredibly thin - much finer than human hair - and typically grow only a few millimeters to a centimeter long. This rare algae is so small that you'll need a magnifying glass or microscope to truly appreciate its intricate structure.

idTips.label: Thread-like filaments
idTips.description: Look for extremely fine, hair-thin green strands floating in still water that feel almost impossibly delicate when touched - like wet spider silk

idTips.label: Radiating pattern
idTips.description: Filaments often spread outward in a star or wheel-spoke pattern when viewed from above, creating small geometric arrangements in the water

idTips.label: Bright green color
idTips.description: Fresh specimens show a vibrant grass-green color that's especially noticeable when backlit by sunlight

idTips.label: Microscopic cells
idTips.description: With magnification, you can see individual barrel-shaped cells joined end-to-end like tiny green train cars

idTips.label: Floating habit
idTips.description: Drifts freely in the water column rather than attaching to rocks or plants, often collecting in quiet corners of ponds

habitat: Found in clean, quiet freshwater environments like small ponds, slow-moving streams, and temporary pools in New England's forests and wetlands. Prefers nutrient-poor to moderately nutrient-rich waters with good light penetration. Often discovered in small woodland pools, beaver ponds, or the calm backwaters of gentle streams where water movement is minimal.

seasonality.spring: Most active during spring warming when daylight increases and water temperatures rise, forming new filaments as ice melts from quiet pools.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season when filaments are most visible and abundant, especially in July and August during warm, sunny weather.
seasonality.fall: Populations begin to decline as temperatures cool and daylight decreases, though some filaments may persist into early autumn.
seasonality.winter: Largely dormant or absent from the water column, surviving as resting stages in sediments until spring conditions return.

funFact: Despite being incredibly rare with only two confirmed sightings in all of New England, each tiny filament of Radiofilum conjunctivum can contain hundreds of individual cells that communicate with each other through microscopic channels, essentially making each strand a living telegraph wire!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other thread-like green algae like Spirogyra, but Radiofilum's radiating growth pattern and much finer filaments help distinguish it - think of Spirogyra as green yarn while Radiofilum is more like green silk thread.
contextualKnowledge: This algae is so uncommon that many professional botanists have never encountered it in the field, making any sighting scientifically noteworthy and worth reporting to local naturalist groups or universities.
compareHints: As the only Radiofilum species known from New England, it's best compared to other members of the Sphaeropleaceae family like Sphaeroplea, but Radiofilum forms much shorter, more delicate filaments and lacks the distinctive reproductive structures that make Sphaeroplea look like green necklaces. Radiofilum's radiating growth pattern is also unique among New England's thread-like algae.
